subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Suraj had promised the client the demo on Friday at ten, and the demo needed the data Sunaina had said would arrive on Thursday. On Thursday afternoon her message came: “Almost there, tomorrow morning for sure.” Suraj felt his stomach sink. He called the client to ask for a later slot, moved two colleagues off other work to build a stand-in dataset overnight, and cancelled his own dinner plan. The real data came on Saturday. On Monday Suraj wrote Sunaina's next promised date on the team board with a small question mark beside it, and added two days in his own private notes. “It's not that it slipped,” he told his partner. “It's that I can't rely on her dates now.”

qa.q: What did Suraj do when Sunaina said the data would come tomorrow morning?
qa.a: Suraj called the client for a later slot, moved two colleagues to build a stand-in dataset overnight and cancelled his dinner plan.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel when Sunaina's message came?
qa.a: Suraj's stomach sank: he felt alarmed and let down because the demo depended on the data.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do differently when giving her next date?
qa.a: Give an honest, longer estimate with a warning as soon as the date looks unsafe, so Suraj can plan around it.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's colleagues feel about the overnight work?
qa.a: The two colleagues moved off their own work probably feel tired and annoyed at the sudden reshuffle, and may also start doubting Sunaina's dates.

grounding: A person relies on another's promised date and has to reshuffle everything when it slips, and trust erodes.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Salma checked the shared sheet for the third time that week. The vendor onboarding was Kishore's job, and Kishore's date had been “Monday”, then “Wednesday”, then “definitely Friday”. Each promise sounded cheerful, and each time Salma had booked the training room and told the finance team to expect the vendor's account. Each time she had rebooked. This Friday the room was booked again, and again the message came at 5 pm: “Some paperwork pending, sorry!” Salma read it twice, closed the laptop and sat silently for a moment. Then she wrote in the sheet next to Kishore's name a line she would never have added before: “Ask for a real date and what could go wrong.”

qa.q: What dates did Kishore give for the vendor onboarding?
qa.a: Kishore said “Monday”, then “Wednesday”, then “definitely Friday”.

qa.q: What does Salma feel as she reads the message twice and sits quietly?
qa.a: Salma feels frustrated and let down, and her trust in Kishore's dates is wearing thin.

qa.q: What could Kishore do so the next date is believable?
qa.a: Look at how long onboarding really took before, give a longer honest date, and say early if any paperwork could delay it.

qa.q: How might the finance team feel about waiting for the account?
qa.a: The finance team may be confused and irritated after being told to expect the vendor account three times, which would cost them trust in the plan.

grounding: Repeated optimistic dates force a coordinator to rebook and reshuffle, and trust wears away.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Sangeeta ran a small app-testing team from a co-working floor in Hyderabad. On Monday her colleague Usha had promised, "The login module will be ready by Wednesday, no problem." Sangeeta built the week around it: testers booked for Thursday, a client demo on Friday. On Wednesday evening Usha messaged: "Need two more days, sorry!" Sangeeta sat back, jaw tight. This was the third time. She called the testers to move their slot, emailed the client, and reworked the sprint board till nine. The next morning she asked Usha, gently but firmly, "Next time, give me the date you'd bet on, not the one you hope for."

qa.q: By when had Usha promised the login module?
qa.a: Usha promised it would be ready by Wednesday.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when the message came?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and let down, sitting back with her jaw tight, because this was the third time.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta ask for, and why could it help?
qa.a: She asked for the date Usha would bet on, not the hoped-for one, so the team can plan around an honest estimate.

qa.q: How might Usha feel hearing Sangeeta's request?
qa.a: Usha might feel embarrassed but also relieved that a longer, honest date is now welcome without it being seen as weakness.

grounding: Shows a team lead who relied on a colleague's promised date having to reshuffle everything when it slips again.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
Aditi: "Kavitha, how's the budget sheet? The board meeting is tomorrow at ten."
Kavitha: "Almost done! Tonight for sure."
Aditi: "You said that on Monday."
Kavitha: "I know, but the sales numbers came late."
Aditi: "Then why didn't you tell me on Monday? I told the director it was ready."
Kavitha: "I thought I'd catch up."
Aditi: "I've now moved the presentation order twice. I had to ask Rohit to prepare a backup slide."
Kavitha: "I'm sorry."
Aditi: "I'm not angry that it's late. Things get late. I'm upset that I couldn't plan around it."
Kavitha: "So what should I do?"
Aditi: "Give me a longer date I can trust. I'd rather hear Friday and get Friday."

qa.q: When is the board meeting?
qa.a: The board meeting is tomorrow at ten.

qa.q: What is Aditi feeling, and why?
qa.a: Aditi is upset and let down, not about the delay itself, but because there was no way to plan around it after being told it was nearly done.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do next time a deadline starts to slip?
qa.a: Tell Aditi as soon as the numbers come late and give a longer, honest date instead of hoping to catch up.

qa.q: How does Kavitha seem to see the situation?
qa.a: Kavitha seems sorry and a bit defensive, genuinely believing there was time to catch up and not seeing the cost to Aditi's planning.

grounding: A dialogue shows a team lead forced to reshuffle because a colleague kept giving optimistic dates.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: I'm Imran, and I lead a small support team. Last quarter Farhan was building our new ticket dashboard. He's talented, and every week he said, "Two more days." I believed him because I liked him and wanted it to be true. I told my manager it would launch on the 15th. On the 14th, Farhan admitted it needed another week. I had to cancel the training I'd booked, re-brief my manager and apologise to twelve agents. What stung most wasn't the delay. It was that I'd stopped trusting his dates. When we talked, I said I'd rather hear "three weeks" than "two days" five times.

qa.q: When did Imran tell the manager the dashboard would launch?
qa.a: Imran said it would launch on the 15th.

qa.q: What made Imran feel hurt about the delay?
qa.a: Imran felt hurt that trust in Farhan's dates had worn away, which stung more than the delay itself.

qa.q: What would you advise Farhan after this conversation?
qa.a: Give a longer, honest estimate like three weeks and update early if it slips, so Imran can plan without cancelling training.

qa.q: How might the twelve agents see the cancelled training?
qa.a: The agents might feel confused or mildly annoyed, having set time aside for training that suddenly wasn't happening.

grounding: A team lead describes having to reshuffle plans after a colleague's repeated optimistic dates, and losing trust.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
Operations manager's note, Friday.
I watched Nikita, our team lead, have a hard week, and I want to record why.
On Monday, Jaya told Nikita the vendor database would be cleaned by Wednesday. Jaya said this cheerfully and sincerely, the way she has said it before. Nikita built the week around it: training for new staff on Thursday, client reports on Friday.
On Wednesday evening, Jaya said, "Almost done, maybe tomorrow noon." On Thursday it was "end of day." Nikita cancelled the training, apologised to six new staff, and moved the client reports to Monday. I saw her rub her eyes at her desk at seven.
This is the third time this quarter. Nikita told me quietly, "I'd rather Jaya said Friday and meant it."
I have asked Jaya to give estimates using how long the last similar tasks actually took, and to warn Nikita the moment a date is at risk.
— Operations manager

qa.q: When did Jaya say the vendor database would be cleaned?
qa.a: By Wednesday.

qa.q: How was Nikita feeling by Thursday evening?
qa.a: Nikita was tired and frustrated, rubbing her eyes at her desk after cancelling the training and moving the reports.

qa.q: What has the manager asked Jaya to change, and why?
qa.a: To base estimates on how long similar tasks actually took and to warn early, because repeated optimistic dates keep forcing Nikita to reshuffle.

qa.q: How might Jaya see her own dates?
qa.a: Jaya seems to give each date sincerely and cheerfully, probably believing every time that the task will go smoothly.

grounding: Shows a team lead who relies on a colleague's cheerful dates and has to reshuffle repeatedly, as optimism erodes trust.
